EntertainmentTab.title: Xbox bets on Gears of War: E-Day in battle of gaming giants
EntertainmentTab.text:
Gears of War, one of the video games that helped Microsoft's Xbox to win over millions of fans, is back.

Prequel E-Day takes players back to where it all started, telling the origin story of humanity's conflict with The Locust - the series' horrifying enemy species.

The game's been well-received by critics and players, but it's also seen as a big test of Xbox's new direction.

Unlike recent flagship titles from the company's studios, which have been released on PlayStation 5 and, in some cases, Nintendo Switch, E-Day is being pushed as an Xbox exclusive.

The apparent goal is to draw players back to the brand, but critics have questioned whether that's realistic at a time when console prices are higher than ever.

BBC Newsbeat spoke to developer The Coalition - the makers of E-Day - about what staying exclusive means to them.

Gears of War has been one of Xbox's flagship series since it launched back in 2006.

Creative director Matt Searcy tells Newsbeat the sci-fi shooter is a "mix of war story with comic book-y monsters that come out of the ground".

"It's a video game with a lot of heart, a lot of blood and guts," he says.

First released on the Xbox 360, Gears helped to popularise "cover-shooter" gameplay, which encouraged players to shelter from enemy attacks.

It brought a strategic dimension to third-person action games, and also won fans with its co-operative multiplayer modes - a feature that's returned for E-Day.

But, 20 years later, Xbox finds itself in a very different position in the console space.

It's seen as a third-place competitor, behind both Sony's PlayStation and Nintendo's Switch consoles.

Previous CEO Phil Spencer had begun to take the division in a new direction, releasing some of its most popular games on rival consoles for the first time.

E-Day was widely expected to follow other high budget series such as Halo on to other companies' machines.

But new Xbox boss Asha Sharma, who took over the job in June, announced Gears of War would remain a "console exclusive", although a PC version has also been released.

Her strategy has been called into question by critics.

After taking six years to make and an estimated budget in the hundreds of millions, they argue that keeping E-Day away from other platforms could mean it's less likely to make back its development cost.

Coalition studio head Mike Crump says E-Day is a "natural choice to be an exclusive".

"Gears has been an exclusive franchise to Xbox for 20 years now. It's sort of entwined deeply with the brand," he says.

"And we're proud of that."

He says the series "carries the banner" for the console and gives people a "reason to be in the Xbox ecosystem" - something he says has been the company's mission since day one.

However, there will inevitably be discourse around E-Day's sales figures and engagement numbers.

When asked what would constitute success for the game, Crump admits the studio has financial targets and goals for the number of players it wants to reach, but insists it takes a "broader view" than that.

"We measure things like, are we showcasing the platform? Are we pushing the hardware to its limits? Are we showcasing what the Xbox is capable of?

"Our goal basically is to be the best-looking game on the Xbox and really show the industry what's possible with our hardware."

Crump also says it's important to drive players towards Game Pass, Xbox's Netflix-style subscription service.

For onlookers, it's harder to ignore the wider picture at Xbox.

The division has been carrying out mass layoffs and undergoing a wide-scale restructuring since Sharma's appointment.

In July, she told employees there would be 3,200 job losses across Xbox-owned studios over the current financial year.

Last month, the company said it was about three-quarters of the way through this plan, external.

The Coalition has mostly avoided cuts so far, although one of E-Day's narrative directors announced last month he had been let go.

Reports have suggested developers at the studio are worried they could be at risk now the game has been released, external.

When asked about this, Crump says: "What I say to myself, what I say to the team, is we just we need to focus on the things that we can control.

"For us that's about shipping a great game that people are going to love and I feel like, as a team, we've done that."

He says E-Day will provide a "great foundation" for future games in the series, and insists "the next game will not take nearly as long" to make.

Developers at other studios hit by layoffs previously told the BBC they were concerned about a loss of institutional knowledge - experienced staff who've been working on certain series for years and sometimes decades.

Crump says: "We've got a great team here.

"And the leadership team in particular has worked together for upwards of 20 years.

"So there's definitely a continuity of knowledge and experience."

EntertainmentTab.title: Carrie: Is Prime Video's adaptation still relevant in 2026?
EntertainmentTab.text:
Adaptations, remakes and reboots are all the rage right now, and there’s often one question that crops up - why?

See also "what's the point?" and "do we need another one?" whenever a story is resurrected from the past.

Carrie, Prime Video's new TV series based on Stephen King's debut novel, has been no exception.

It's not the first time the tale of high school bullies and supernatural powers has been adapted for the screen.

Director Brian de Palma's 1976 movie version is a horror classic, with some of its most famous scenes and imagery widely considered iconic within the genre.

But the cast and creator of the latest version, which drags Carrie's story forward 50 years into a world of social media, have been telling BBC Newsbeat why they believe it's still relevant in 2026.

Fans of the novel have been quick to complain the new version of Carrie is not "book accurate", pointing out that she was originally an abrasive, even unlikeable character.

In the TV adaptation, Carrie has been raised behind closed doors by her paranoid father and deeply religious mother, and only enters school after a tragedy reveals her existence to authorities.

Audiences see a different version of the character in the show - one who's naive, but open and eager to learn new things.

"There's a lot of opinions, and I purposely avoided the original movie and and the book before filming because I hadn't seen it or read it," Summer H Howell, who plays Carrie, tells Newsbeat.

"And I wanted to create this new, light version of Carrie that was excited to get out of her house and just curious about the world and people."

However, the 22-year-old actress says the journey her character goes on is not so different, and argues it's still relevant today.

"It's the story of an outsider, and bullying has not gone away in 50 years," she says.

"If anything, it's just gotten worse with social media."

Social media plays a huge part in the adaptation by horror director Mike Flanagan, who's best known for series such as The Haunting of Hill House.

In his version of Carrie, some of the most famous scenes, including the dramatic prom moment, are adapted to a world where everything is filmed and shared online.

Alison Thornton, who plays chief bully Chris Hargensen, says social media "is kind of a villain in the show".

"You can post something, or someone will take a video of something, and the fact that it can be permanently online is actually quite terrifying," she says.

Thornton says the adaptation aims to show how online posts can have "repercussions in real life".

Showrunner Flanagan tells Newsbeat it would have been "impossible to ignore the impact social media has had in changing the way we see each other".

Fifty years ago, he says, bullying would have been relatively "private", and confined to "the classroom, in the halls, in the school".

But that's all changed, says Flanagan.

"It's happening with the audience of the entire digital world and enshrined forever, permanently on these platforms.

"It's a whole different ball game that way," he says.

Carrie is the latest project from Prime Video targeted at Gen Z viewers based on a popular novel.

The Summer I Turned Pretty, Your Fault: London, and Off Campus have been huge hits for the streamer, and it's leaned into trends such as BookTok to generate interest in the shows.

Josie Totah, who plays Chris's sidekick Tina, agrees remakes and adaptations are popular, but says she would only get involved with one if the "intention" felt right.

"No one wants to just remake something for the sake of remaking it," she says.

"'Why now?' - unless that can be answered thoroughly, I don't think that I would want to do it."

There are worries from fans that revisiting existing works leaves less space for original stories.

Totah says projects such as this year's indie horror hit Obsession also deserve to be championed.

"Those are equally as important as the ones that we've already told in the past, if not maybe a little bit more," she says.

So far, Flanagan's version of Carrie has had a mostly positive response from critics, with an 85% positive rating on review website Rotten Tomatoes.

Most praised the performances and social commentary, although some reviewers felt it wasn't as scary as earlier versions and accused it of sanding down some of the original characters' harder edges.

The verdict from fans remains to be seen.

Flanagan hasn't just expanded on the original story, but has also made some fairly major changes, possibly laying the ground for further series to be made.

"I try to think about how fans will feel because I'm a Stephen King fan first," he says.

"So I have very strong opinions about changes that are made in adaptation."

Flanagan has brought other Stephen King novels to the screen before, but those have tended to be much more faithful to the source material.

Some of his best-known projects, reinventions of The Haunting of Hill House by author Shirley Jackson and The Fall of the House of Usher by Edgar Allan Poe, have been based on works by long-deceased authors.

"I've just never done this with an author who's still alive or one with whom I already have a very intensely productive working relationship," he says.

"I hope people are going to look at these changes and say: 'Oh, this is actually why it makes good sense to tell this story again today'."

Carrie will launch on Prime Video on 7 October

EntertainmentTab.title: King Charles and Elton John in the audience for Apple music workshop
EntertainmentTab.text:
King Charles has visited a hi-tech music workshop for young people, in a collaboration between his King's Trust charity and technology firm Apple.

Pop royalty, in the form of Sir Elton John, was a special guest at the event, sitting beside the King, as they listened to a short performance from singer-songwriter Skye Newman.

The event was held at a music hall in Apple's headquarters building, in the restored Battersea Power Station in south west London.

The project being backed by the King is intended to equip young people with practical skills to work in the creative industries.

The King was introduced to Prophet Guillory, Apple Music's head of artist services, tools and community, who was praised for his work as a mentor for young people.

"Wow, you did your homework," Prophet said, when the King seemed familiar with his efforts.

The King was introduced to young performers at the event.

Another young musician said the problem was getting the money together to launch creative ideas.

Young performer Skye Newman faced what must have seemed like a very unusual X-Factor style panel - King Charles, Sir Elton, his husband David Furnish and Apple's executive chairman Tim Cook.

The music workshop was part of a project between Apple and the King's Trust Creative Labs, and is the latest link-up between the royals and the Californian tech giant.

Last year, the King revealed a playlist of 17 of his favourite tracks, which was issued on Apple Music.

The King didn't include Sir Elton John in any of those choices - but the pop star has been a long-time supporter of the King's Trust charity, which was previously known as the Prince's Trust.

Now in its 50th year, the charity was set up to give opportunities to deprived and marginalised young people - and has so far helped 1.3 million people across the UK.

The tie-up with Apple shows the changing demands for work skills, including using the latest technology for young people wanting to build careers in the music and creative industries.

There was also a royal link with Battersea Power Station - as that had once provided the electricity for Buckingham Palace.

In the power station's control room, the link to the Palace had been discreetly labelled as "Carnaby Street", in case any intruders had ever been tempted to switch off the Palace lights.

EntertainmentTab.title: Jeffrey Archer: Queen Camilla pays tribute to 'irrepressible' author and former politician
EntertainmentTab.text:
Queen Camilla has paid tribute to the bestselling author and former politician Jeffrey Archer, who has died at the age of 86.

"Seldom does an author get to live a life as rich, varied and colourful as any of the characters in their books, or with as many surprising plot twists," the Queen said in a statement.

She added that Archer was "not without flaw", but that "friends will recall him as an irrepressible life force through all the many differing chapters of his life".

The former Conservative MP was jailed for perjury in 2001 after being found guilty of lying and cheating in his 1987 libel case against the Daily Star.

The Queen said he was "an exception to the end" and that it was "with sadness that I learned of his death yesterday, on the eve of publication of his final work and so soon after appearing at my Queen's Reading Room Festival".

Archer was a supporter of the Queen's Reading Room charity.

"My sympathies go to Mary and the family at this time of sorrow. I hope it may be some consolation for them to know what pleasure Jeffrey brought to me and to so many millions of readers through the pages of his works.

"Wherever the next page turns to, I trust there will be champagne and Shepherd's Pie in abundance. Camilla R."

Archer's parties were known for serving champagne and shepherd's pie to guests.

Archer sold more than 300 million books in his five-decade writing career, including the Clifton Chronicles and Kane and Abel, and often set the novels in his home town of Wellington, Somerset.

In a statement, Archer's publisher HarperCollins said the author died "suddenly and peacefully at home" on Monday between writing sessions.

Archer was born in north London in 1940 but soon moved to Weston-super-Mare in Somerset and in 1969, Archer was elected MP for the Lincolnshire constituency of Louth.

He served as an MP for five years before becoming Conservative Party deputy chairman.

He moved to the House of Lords in 1992 but was jailed for four years for perjury and perverting the course of justice in 2001.

He was found to have lied in libel action he had brought against the Daily Star newspaper, in which he was awarded £500,000 in damages.

The Star had alleged Archer had slept with a sex worker.

The peer was found by the court to have perverted the course of justice by asking a former friend to give him a false alibi and producing fake diary entries to back up his story.

He was also found to have perjured himself on oath during the libel trial.

He was released from jail in 2003 and returned to the House of Lords until he retired in 2024.

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch described Archer's death as "devastating news".

"We will miss him very much," she told BBC Breakfast on Tuesday, adding that he had texted her earlier on Monday.

Badenoch said he was "very much loved by the Conservative family", adding: "I'm glad that I saw him recently."

Speaking about what she described as "other parts of his life", she said: "He did serve his time, he made amends, and he wanted to do a lot of good in the world."

Former Conservative prime minister Sir John Major said "we have lost a man who lived one of the most remarkable lives of our age", and that he will be "much missed – and long remembered".

Archer's last novel, Adam and Eve, was released on Tuesday.

Broadcaster Gyles Brandreth told BBC Breakfast that he was with Archer on Sunday. "I mean, literally 72 hours ago, doing a show in the West End of London celebrating this book, the publication, and he was in great form.

"He didn't really acknowledge that he'd changed much since being in prison, but I think he became a nicer person in some ways, a gentler, a milder person after the prison experience."

Former Conservative Party leader Iain Duncan Smith described Archer as "a remarkable man who did everything at full bore", adding: "There were simply no half measures with him."

Other former ministers also paid tribute. Sajid Javid said Archer had been a "dear friend", while Sir Jeremy Hunt said Archer had "showed enormous kindness with his advice about how to become a writer".

James Cleverly said the author and politician had been "a huge personality and fantastic storyteller", and that he had been very supportive when his wife Suzie was recovering from cancer.

Reform UK member and former Conservative minister Nadim Zahawi, wrote: "Jeffrey Archer was a dear friend and an extraordinary human being. His gift for storytelling was matched by his wit, warmth and boundless energy. Life was never dull in Jeffrey's company."

Last week, Archer returned to his former school to promote his last book.

"It's wonderful to come back. What I got a real thrill about when I was walking towards the library is seeing the young boys and girls and thinking, 'that's the next generation'," Archer said at Wellington School.

Archer had been due to attend the Cheltenham Literature Festival on Saturday to discuss his final novel.

He and his wife Mary had celebrated their 60th wedding anniversary this year, HarperCollins said.

The couple have two sons and five grandchildren.

EntertainmentTab.title: BBC Time writer Jimmy McGovern calls young offenders staff lazy
EntertainmentTab.text:
Bafta-winning screenwriter Jimmy McGovern has said going into young offender institutions to research his new drama left him believing that keeping inmates isolated from each other for long periods allowed staff to "sit on their backsides all day and do nothing".

McGovern said he was shocked after visiting "appalling" facilities while researching the latest series of his BBC drama Time.

He told BBC North West Tonight those in young offender institutions (YOIs) were "banged up 23 hours a day" as part of a policy to stop offenders mixing, which gave officers an "excuse for being lazy".

The Prison Officers' Association (POA) said that criticism was "unfair" to call officers lazy - and the policy was essential due to a daily threat of serious violence.

Liverpool-born McGovern focused on adult prison estates in the first two series of BBC hit Time.

But his third series, which sees a young cast star alongside David Tennant and Siobhan Finneran, follows young offenders through a system which McGovern said had "got to be better".

In researching the series, which he wrote with Samuel Bailey, McGovern decided to get a behind-the-scenes look inside real-life YOIs.

He said what he witnessed left him "truly shocked".

"It is absolutely appalling," he said.

"There's young boys with enormous energy banged up 23 hours a day [and] not allowed out of the cells.

"They call them rooms, but they're cells.

"And that's because of the keep-apart system."

The keep-aparts policy is a method of separating young offenders in a bid to cut down on violence.

The separation of young people in YOIs has been a topic of debate for a number of years - with the most recent review from HM Inspectorate of Prisons finding some held in YOIs were not permitted to leave their cells at all on some days, external.

McGovern said he recognised a need for "regimentation" in YOIs, but said he believed keep-aparts had increased following lockdown measures imposed during the Covid-19 pandemic.

He said he believed the policy had allowed officers to avoid their duties.

"It allows officers to sit on their backsides all day and do nothing," he said.

"This happened before Covid, but Covid gave them the excuse to keep them banged up even more.

"After Covid, they didn't want to see the kids, so it became worse."

He said he did not believe an increased use of the policy was due to staffing and funding challenges.

"I'm afraid they're lazy," he said.

"I've met wonderful prison officers, but I've seen some lazy ones and the keep-apart system enables them to be lazy with an excuse for being lazy."

He said officers should be able to handle fights among the offenders and described conditions as "feral".

"They're young boys bursting with energy [being] cooped up," he said.

"When they get out, they want to fight, but [the staff] are prison officers. They should be able to handle that."

He said he understood how "tough" the job was and that the young offenders in the facilities were "very, very difficult, so there has to be an element of regimentation [and] rules and regulations... but that's your job".

He said officers at YOIs were "paying the price" of a lack of investment and staffing and it was "unfair to suggest staff are lazy".

"They are stretched to breaking point by chronic under-staffing and unmanageable workloads," he said.

"Without serious investment in staffing, facilities and rehabilitation, we will continue to see violent and chaotic YOIs - and prison officers paying the price."

The Ministry of Justice said it did not "recognise these claims about our hardworking prison staff".

"Their dedication helps ensure young offenders are punished as appropriate while being supported into rehabilitation, and we will deliver on our commitment to give children in prison more time outside their room," a spokesperson said.

EntertainmentTab.title: Free Winnie-the-Pooh books to fill phone box libraries
EntertainmentTab.text:
Free books for 150 red phone box libraries are being made available to celebrate 100 years of two British legends - Winnie-the-Pooh and the K2 red phone box.

The story's original publisher, Farshore, said it would donate copies of AA Milne's classics - whose setting was inspired by Ashdown Forest in East Sussex - alongside a new authorised sequel A Little Boy and His Bear.

Sally Phillips, actor and narrator of the newly reissued Winnie-the-Pooh audiobooks, launched the campaign earlier by reading to schoolchildren at a phone box library in Chartham, Kent.

"He has always been the number one bear in our house," she told the BBC.

People across the UK have been invited to nominate their local red phone box libraries for the books to help the campaign's organisers "uncover more hidden gems".

Nominations have been opened to phone boxes which have already been adapted into community libraries, with libraries in Derbyshire, Hertfordshire, Leicestershire and the West Midlands having already signed up.

Phillips said there was a lot to love about the bear's view of life, both for children and adults.

She said the books were "great to read as an adult because they're really funny, much funnier than you remember.

"When you read them to children, you remember how much kid-friendly drama there is in them."

EntertainmentTab.title: Disney accuses Trump officials of ‘blatant violations’ of constitution amid FCC battle
EntertainmentTab.text:
Lawyers for Disney accused the Trump administration of “blatant violations of the US constitution” and censorship on Tuesday in the first court hearing over the Federal Communications Commission’s early review of the media giant’s eight local television station licenses.

District judge Loren AliKhan seemed unswayed by government arguments that the order to force Disney’s ABC to apply years early to renew local television station licenses was tied to an investigation into parent company Disney’s hiring practices.

ABC, Disney and its station group filed suit against the FCC in August, seeking to block the US media regulator from taking any further steps to punish or pressure the network in connection to the order.

In its lawsuit, ABC argued that the FCC’s actions – taken at the behest of the Donald Trump-appointed chair, Brendan Carr – were actually intended to chill the network’s speech, which the president and Carr have argued is tilted against the administration.

In legal filings and during Tuesday’s hearing, the network cited past threats by the president and the FCC chairman that jeopardized the licenses of television networks, including ABC on several occasions, for editorial purposes.

“These are blatant violations of the US constitution,” the prominent trial lawyer Beth Wilkinson, arguing on behalf of ABC, told the judge during the approximately two-hour hearing.

She said ABC faced a “chilling effect” that has affected – and will continue to impact – its editorial decision-making, as the network steers clear of political bookings and any other programming decisions that could spark further ire from the Trump administration and Carr. “That chilling effect has been happening and will happen every day,” she said, causing “irreparable harm” to the network and its ability to broadcast independent news for the benefit of the American people.

ABC has said it has stopped booking politicians on the daytime talkshow The View and chose to air a July speech by Trump on its streaming platform so as not to antagonize the president. “Our editorial decisions are being affected right now,” Wilkinson said, noting the significance of decisions about how to cover next month’s pivotal midterm elections. “We are watching everything we do … We have already altered our conduct because of the fear of retaliation.”

She also noted that ABC recently chose to air a Jimmy Kimmel-conducted interview with Texas US Senate candidate James Talarico on YouTube, rather than television, “because the FCC has no control over YouTube”.

Dimitar P Georgiev, representing the FCC defendants, argued that “there is no reason to believe the early renewal order has prompted changes to the plaintiffs’ editorial decisions”. He also argued that the US district court for the District of Columbia was not the proper jurisdiction for the case, saying that ABC could instead appeal any adverse decision to the US court of appeals for the District of Columbia.

ABC is seeking a decision from the judge to enjoin the FCC from taking any further actions against the network’s licenses. “We are asking to stop pure retaliation, putting us in a process that we should never have to be in,” Wilkinson said.

In what Wilkinson called a “fatal admission”, Georgiev said the license renewal process “is not about the licenses”, but is instead a “tool” to expedite the commission’s review of ABC for potential violations of federal equal opportunities regulations. The lawyer also said the FCC could choose to end the license review process early if ABC is able to satisfy its document requests.

Considering that the FCC opened its employment practice investigation into Disney last year, with requests for documents ongoing since then, the judge asked: “Why is it only in the summer that you determined that their responses were woefully inadequate?”

She also questioned why the commission required the company to submit renewal applications for all eight of its stations simultaneously.

And she noted past comments by Carr about the network’s licenses, including a remark in July, when he had said ABC’s decision not to carry the president’s speech that month on its linear channel could factor into the license investigation.

“It strikes me with all the comments that this was merely over a discovery dispute, what made this so different that you needed to call for an early license renewal?” Judge AliKhan asked lawyers for the FCC, whom she asked for a list of some of the other enforcement actions the commission could have taken short of calling up the network’s licenses early.

And she noted that there was “some daylight” in the FCC’s arguments, considering that the diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) inquiry was handled by the commission’s enforcement bureau, while the license order was made by the media bureau.

The judge ended the hearing without issuing an order, saying she would take the matter “under advisement”.

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘In the wake of death, Courtney Love was giving it her all’: Hole’s Melissa auf der Maur on her best photograph
EntertainmentTab.text:
When I was going through the archives for my rock photo book, I came across my first ever self-portrait, at Père Lachaise Cemetery in Paris, in front of Jim Morrison’s grave. I am a 13-year-old on an awkward trip with my cool father. He had no respect or interest in Jim Morrison, and that photo is like every photo I’ve taken from that moment on – I’m trying to take agency over what is happening. Photography was the absolute first thing that gave me a feeling of having my own say. It became a way of creating my own universe, one that I could trust. It was absolutely my first love.

I was sidetracked into music in a beautiful way by these radical women and a countercultural movement, so the subject of my photographs just changed. It was me within this environment, on stage with Hole, backstage with these luminary, wild people, travelling across the world. My photography followed and morphed with me, and my camera documented my generation being hijacked by corporate greed and destroyed in the wake of the sacrificial death of Kurt Cobain. It was a generational call to document the Lollapalooza ’95 tour, where this photo was taken, for us to understand later. It was also when the wild alternative freaks crossed into the mainstream.

Bass players are natural wallflowers and I always had a camera with me, just like everyone has a phone now. In terms of my duty as a female photographer in Hole – not a girlfriend, not an outside male photographer – I was able to glean the essence of that band through that misunderstood and wildly celebrated, but also dismantled queen, Courtney. What I love about the photos of her, and in this photo where she’s just doing her makeup, getting ready to go on stage, is she trusted me so implicitly. She either didn’t notice the camera, or she gave herself to the camera, so I was able to capture her true essence, in the same way that she trusted me to be her bass player and right-hand woman. My camera and I got to just drink that in.

Courtney had been asked to do a tour diary of Lollapalooza for Spin magazine, so it was natural they asked me to take the photos. It felt really grown up for a 23-year-old. I was capturing the humanity, mystery and happiness – as much reality as possible to unpack later, understanding that time and distance would give me perspective. I had bought a new camera for the road, a Nikon point-and-shoot, because my manual camera was not cutting it on tour. It was a camera that could adapt to the subject changing quickly, and shit was happening quick. The wide-angle lens was a revelation, because my little hand could get the giant ocean of crowd, and I could also fit four people in a frame.

This photo captures the spirit of the people who were central to this story in a very particular way, which is kind of how it landed on the cover of this book. It was near the end of the three-week tour; I have a whole roll that I took this day. I would always photograph us right before going on stage, unless shit was bad, so the fact I have half a roll of that moment means we were obviously feeling very strong that night. That is rare in a band that was living in the wake of death, with the struggles of addiction and with enemies on the tour. The fact I was confident enough to take our photo so much makes me think it was a very happy day on what should have been a very happy time in our band. We were at the peak of our alternative power, co-headlining with Sonic Youth, and Courtney was giving her all. Her life was an absolute nightmare – and there was a rivalry with Sonic Youth, who were the gatekeepers of cool at that moment – but she was giving her all on this tour.

My life in the band was the defining role of that decade for me. Yes, I was later in the Smashing Pumpkins, and yes, I was an art photographer too, but my life in Hole defined me spiritually, emotionally, musically, and also publicly. Courtney, obviously, is infamous and misunderstood, but my portraits of her in this book are loving and true.

Melissa Auf der Maur: My ’90s Rock Photographs is published by DelMonico Books. It accompanies the exhibition at Art Gallery of Ontario, until 6 June 2027.

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘He was devastatingly sexy’: Frasier’s Jane Leeves and David Hyde Pierce on the love between Daphne and Niles
EntertainmentTab.text:
“Dr Crane, your glockenspiel has sprung to life!”

It was a crush. An unexpected one. The psychiatrist Niles Crane (snooty, conflict-avoidant, married to a high-society wife with a fear of buffets) fell for his father’s physio, Daphne Moon (working class, Mancunian, reckons she’s a bit psychic) the moment he met her in his brother’s Seattle apartment.

Across seven seasons of the mega-sitcom Frasier, the crush took hold. Daphne remained seemingly oblivious, but the pair built a friendship and a will-they-won’t-they story that fans loved to be teased with. It made for some cracking episodes: from the pair being holed up in Niles’ candlelit mansion during a rainstorm (with that broken glockenspiel) in the side-splitting A Mid-Winter Night’s Dream, to a passionate leg-in-the-air tango after Niles’ divorce in Moon Dance (“Oh mama, I’ve got it all!”).

Daphne finally learned the truth the night before her wedding to Donny. The next morning, in her white gown, she knocked on the Winnebago in which Niles (four days into a bad new marriage himself) was hiding and told him to drive.

“Fasten your seatbelt, Daphne.”

“Fasten yours, Niles.”

It’s been 22 years since we last saw the pair on screen, but the stars Jane Leeves and David Hyde Pierce remain dear friends. Hyde Pierce attended – and had a near fatal car accident at – Leeves’ English wedding and he is godfather to her son. They are both in long-term marriages: Hyde Pierce and the writer-producer Brian Hargrove married in 2008 after 25 years together; Leeves and the TV executive Marshall Coben have been married for 30 years. In fact, John Mahoney, who played Marty Crane in Frasier, predicted Leeves’ relationship one day in the green room: “I always wanted kids and said to John: ‘I’m going to adopt,’” she remembers. “He said: ‘Do not do that now. Within a year, you will meet someone.’ And she did, at a Paramount party. “I don’t know how that happened.”

“I love you doing this,” Leeves laughs from her Malibu kitchen, as Hyde Pierce joins from a study (which features a bookcase Niles would be proud of) in his New York home. He claims to have just had his hair done – endearingly, he’s a bit frazzled – before asking for reassurance that no one will see this video. They’re more than happy, though, to tell the story of Daphne and Niles.

Do you remember meeting for the first time?

Jane Leeves: I was on the set on the first day of the pilot and I saw David walking in and crossing the bleachers. I went racing up to him like a mad fan because I’d been watching [the Washington-DC-based sitcom] The Powers That Be, which was cancelled for some bizarre reason – it was brilliant and he played the most odd and fabulous character. I don’t think you really had any dialogue, did you?

David Hyde Pierce: No, I played a suicidal congressman who only mumbled.

JL: I thought there was a calmness, a kindness and an intellect that was devastatingly sexy, I have to say.

DHP: Well, I thought: I can’t believe Paramount Studios doesn’t have security … No, I realised that I lucked out getting the best loon in the business.

JL: A couple of lunatics.

DHP: I knew her from Seinfeld and Murphy Brown – another show from the dark ages. And we just felt like kindred spirits. It’s safe to say that was true of the whole cast. They put a real family together.

JL: It was extraordinary, because I was the only person at that first table read who had read with Kelsey [Grammer]. So the chemistry was unknown.

DHP: Also, we did a photoshoot before the pilot and I remember Jane saying something about how there could be just a little something between us, and we ended up leaning on each other.

JL: I was pulling your tie.

DHP: Yes, and I liked it.

JL: The idea came into my head that they were polar opposites and it would be funny if he found her attractive – because she was also the opposite of Maris.

What was your real relationship like off camera?

JL: Contentious.

DHP: A lot of sex.

JL: I love David. He’s a true gentleman in every sense of the word and the finest human being you’ll ever meet.

DHP: It was as it is now. We’re just best friends. Jane and her husband, Marshall, rented this wonderful shack near the ocean in Malibu. My husband and I, and our dog, would go over and stay. When they moved on, they talked to the landlord about us taking over the rental and we did that. We were very close.

JL: John Mahoney was asking me for my parents’ address [in East Grinstead, West Sussex] one time – he wanted to send them a card – and I read it out. And David went: “Muffin-on-Poot?” and the whole room just fell apart.

DHP: As a person from the US, everything is “something-upon-something” in the UK. That one just occurred to me and it seemed to stick. But it was with great affection.

What do Daphne and Niles love about each other?

DHP: For Niles, Daphne is far and above the most beautiful woman he’s ever seen in his life. Whatever aura she gives off just mesmerises him: her personality, the scent of her hair. He’s bewitched. He also thinks she’s completely beyond him, like a creature from another planet or from mythology or the woodlands or something. The fact that the relationship impossibly comes together is a beautiful surprise for him.

JL: For Daphne, it’s the kindness and gentleness. He’s so different from any man she’s ever experienced. She came from a family with seven brothers, these brutes, so to find that a man could be kind, an intellectual … it’s the same thing for her, it’s this magical man in front of her.

We kept the suspense of the Niles attraction to Daphne going for years and people often ask me: “Why did she not know?” Yes, part of her thought that [he liked her], but the other part of her would say: “Oh, what are you talking about? He’s married and look where you come from and look who he is. He’s a doctor, for goodness sake.” And that voice in the back of her head is what made sense of that seven years of longing.

DHP: The tango in Moon Dance was amazing.

JL: We rehearsed at lightning speed for that. [The episode was written for the pair last minute as Grammer was on “blue flu” strike to negotiate his contract. Unusually, eight of the show’s writers each wrote a part of the script. Grammer returned in time to direct and appear in short scenes.] We had to rehearse with a choreographer. I remember going to David’s house, because we were loving it so much, to rehearse at the weekend. [The director] Jimmy Burrows would have been appalled.

DHP: Our late, great director was famous for not wanting people to rehearse because he had such a keen sense of the rehearsal timeframe of a situation comedy, which is not like rehearsing for a play that’s going to run for months. Even the dog [Moose, who played Eddie] suffered if he learned the trick too soon – it would be ruined and he wouldn’t be able to recreate it in front of the live audience. Jimmy was very big on: “Don’t think it out too much beforehand, because it will blossom at the right moment.”

JL: I love the scene between us [in Mixed Doubles] when Daphne has been dating a Niles lookalike – he breaks up with her and runs off with Niles’ date – and Niles comes to tell Daphne. There’s a wonderful, sweet, gentle scene between them, like shades of Casablanca. [“If it’d been a different time in both our lives, we might actually have met. How do you suppose that would have gone?” Daphne asks him. “I would have said: ‘What are you doing for the rest of your life?’” he replies. They both, as friends, say they love each other.] It was such great writing – these writers were real romantics.

Is there anything you wish Daphne and Niles had done differently?

JL: Seven years is a long time and I think the audience was sort of begging to please bring this to a conclusion.

DHP: I think we all felt we had played that “these two people didn’t think they deserved each other and didn’t believe that they could ever end up with each other” and there comes a point where you just stop believing that.

One thing that the writers did very smartly: they got us together before people were tired of the suspense. I remember very well – speaking of moments that stick with me – when we kissed in front of the live audience. They lost their minds. That was the moment we finally came together. The creators also knew when to end the series; they ended it before any of us were ready. They didn’t want it to dribble off and have the network or the studio say: “Yeah, you’re done.” They wanted to be able to craft a final season. So I don’t know if there are things we wish they did, but I do think those two things were handled really well.

JL: The only thing I wish had been handled differently was the hiding of my first pregnancy. But those were different times. [When Leeves came back from hiatus, she was pregnant with her first child. Her bump was hidden in the series and in later episodes she was given a weight-gain storyline and sent to a “fat camp”.] Daphne and Niles had just got together. I came back and I was pregnant – and they probably thought it was too early for Daphne to be pregnant and they wanted to explore this relationship. But then again, it might have been interesting if she was!

DHP: I’ve never thought of that, Jane, that’s interesting, so off the rails: the idea that we see them run off together at the end of a season and when they come back they’re having a baby.

When did you realise this was a love story for the ages?

DHP: I don’t know if I ever did think of it as a love story for the ages … love story for the agents?

JL: There was an episode or two of Niles and Daphne every season. They were always such great fun. It wasn’t until season two that I realised this thing has legs. Niles’ reaction to Daphne in the room added another layer to Frasier’s apartment; there was this pushback between Niles, Frasier and their dad, and then Daphne comes in and there’s a whole other thing going on. But yeah, by season two, I realised that they were mining this.

DHP: One of the cool things about it, too, was that it’s such sophisticated writing: knowing not to say anything when you have set up a dynamic between two characters. The whole audience knows, when Daphne walks into a room, exactly what Niles is thinking. And, eventually, vice versa. There could be comedy there, it could be poignant, it could be a million things – but it was not a show where it was a joke a minute, getting three jokes on the page. It was a different style. That’s between all the characters, in some ways. You got to know us so well.

What does romance mean to you and how romantic are you in real life?

JL: Oh my goodness. It’s friendship, it’s respect, it’s love. And admiration. I admire my husband, I admire his character. He’s my best friend. And he’s hot. That helps.

DHP: Are you talking about my husband or your husband?

JL: Oh, both of them, darling.

DHP: All of those things. I was thinking about both Niles and Daphne on the show, and me and Brian, or Jane and Marshall – what is romance? It’s a poetic thing. I think it’s possibility. Even having been together for ever, there’s just this air of possibility that the whole world has, because you are together.

JL: I think I know what you’re saying: being with the right person seems to make everything possible.

DHP: Yeah.

JL: You’ve got a good one, too.

DHP: I agree.

What has been the most intense fan reaction to Daphne and Niles?

JL: We’ve always had such respectful fans. I don’t know if there’s been a wild one!

DHP: One of my favourite was in the States when the show first started to air. It was at a set time on a Thursday night or a Tuesday night: therefore, the people who wanted to watch Frasier watched it because they knew when it was on. But then there was a point where it went into syndication, which meant suddenly it was on reruns. I remember walking down the street in New York City. A garbage truck drove by and one of the guys hanging off the truck shouted: “Yo, Niles!” And I thought: oh, there’s a whole new audience getting to see the show.

JL: I get the same thing in New York – New Yorkers are more open. But I always just get: “Hey, it’s the virgin from Seinfeld.” It’s so bizarre. I’m like: “Not any more …”

Did you keep anything from the set that reminds you of Daphne and Niles?

JL: I kept Daphne’s wedding ring and engagement ring.

DHP: The green room over the years became covered wall to wall with stills from every episode that our production photographer, Gail, took. At the end, we walked through and took pictures that were meaningful to us. [He turns his camera to a photo in his office.] It’s the three of us [him, Leeves and Grammer] at the piano. I’ve got a million more and they’re all around.

JL: We have millions. There’s a little gym upstairs and they cover the walls up there. That was the saddest thing for me, before the show was even over. We hadn’t even started rehearsing that week and people were taking those off the walls. I was like: “No, leave everything this way, I don’t need everything to change.”

DHP: I think Marshall took a load of those [the photos in Leeves’ book]. Those are great.

What can Daphne and Niles teach us about love?

JL: To persevere. Don’t ever give up on the dream. It would have been so easy for Niles or Daphne to say: “Well, that’s just ridiculous.” But Niles never gave up that longing. And so many people were in his ear saying: “Niles, you fool, you’re sticking your knife in the toaster!”

DHP: Love comes when you least expect it and it takes seven years.

JL: But it’s worth it in the end.

Daphne and Me by Jane Leeves with Isabella Kathryn Coben is published in the US on 20 October and in the UK on 5 November (HarperCollins, £22). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply

GeneralTab.title: Kemi Badenoch says Tories would scrap inheritance tax on family homes
GeneralTab.text:
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch has pledged to scrap inheritance tax (IHT) on family homes while also allowing couples to leave £1m tax-free, in her keynote speech at the party's conference in Birmingham.

Badenoch added her ambition would be for a Conservative government to abolish IHT "as soon as we can afford it", but said she could not currently propose this due to spending commitments on defence, prisons and the economy.

Badenoch also used her speech to try to make clear how the Tories differed to Labour and Reform UK.

She pitched them as the "no-nonsense party" compared to the Reform UK "circus" and accused Prime Minister Andy Burnham of wanting to "live in the past".

Rival parties hit back and said the proposals for IHT, which is levied on the value of someone's estate when they die, would prioritise support for wealthier people in the country.

Badenoch arrived in Birmingham's Symphony Hall with a message to Conservative Party members that they face a "battle for the soul of the this nation".

She argued her party is "renewed" and "coming back" as she continued efforts to convince voters that it has changed following an historic defeat at the 2024 general election.

In a nod to those who have defected to Nigel Farage's party, Badenoch said: "The Conservatives have had an export boom of drama queens going to Reform.

"This party is now the no drama party, we are the no-nonsense party."

With the party trailing Labour and Reform in the polls, Badenoch acknowledged that people are "looking through the shop window", they "like what they see" but "not enough of them are buying yet, we need to fix that".

Her inspiration for how to revive a long-standing brand was Marks and Spencer (M&S), saying they have "adapted their style for today's market and people are flooding back".

Badenoch added: "Just like M&S, we must learn from our mistakes, win back trust and make people feel good about our party again."

One of the biggest responses in the room from members came as Badenoch made clear she did not want to do an election deal with Reform.

She described many Reform voters as "our people", adding: "We let them down and we want them to come back home."

Following a section of the speech mocking some of Reform's senior figures, Badenoch said: "To those who say 'unite the right', we are not uniting with that.

"People deserve better than that and we are going to give them better than that. Character, conduct, and standards matter."

She also said she did not want to live in a country run by people who "debate whether my mixed-race children are English".

In one of many jibes aimed at Burnham, Badenoch labelled him a "Paddington Bear prime minister" who was "hoping that the problems will just go away".

In the days ahead of Wednesday's speech, there was widespread speculation that Badenoch would announce changes to IHT.

As the opposition leader neared the end of her 66-minute speech, she said IHT was "supposed to be a tax on the super wealthy" but it is "now a tax on ordinary middle-class families in every corner of our country".

She said: "The next Conservative government will legislate so nobody will ever pay inheritance tax on their family home.

"On top of that, couples would be able to leave an additional £1m tax-free and these changes mean every inheritance tax bill will be cut and the number of families paying inheritance tax will fall by more than half."

The Conservatives have estimated the policy would cost around £6bn a year and believe they have identified £71bn of savings that can be made to government spending, including welfare cuts.

Under the current rules, estates worth more than £325,000, or £500,000 if a home is left to children or grandchildren, can face a 40% tax rate on assets above the threshold.

Married or civil partners can also transfer assets between each other.

In 2023-24, 4.72% of UK deaths resulted in an IHT charge and raised around £7bn for the government.

Badenoch also said her "ambition is to abolish inheritance tax altogether, as soon as we can afford it".

Labour Party chairwoman Bridget Phillipson said: "The Tories haven't changed.

"Kemi Badenoch has shown that the Tories' choice is to do nothing to help ordinary families struggling with the cost of social care, prioritising the wealthiest instead."

Reform UK economy spokesman Robert Jenrick said Badenoch had "chickened out of doing anything big" and is "for the 2%".

The former Tory MP said: "While the Tory Party is offering handouts to multi-millionaires, Reform will give everyone a £500 tax cut by raising the tax-free personal allowance to £15,000.

"The Tory Party is looking after its own in Kensington, Reform is looking after the country."

GeneralTab.title: Conservatives united behind Kemi Badenoch - but party still needs to win over voters
GeneralTab.text:
It is Kemi Badenoch's Conservative Party now.

Implicitly and explicitly, that was the message from the Tories' annual conference, which has wrapped up in Birmingham.

It is a party very much united around her, with no murmurings of dissent about her leadership, which is quite the contrast from a year ago.

The pivot point in her time as Conservative leader so far came in her address to this same gathering 12 months back, when, amid constant chatter about the prospect of Robert Jenrick seeking to topple her, she won over the party faithful with an address that oozed confidence.

Not just that. Us reporters were given her speech script, allowing us to follow it line-by-line to help us report what she has said quickly and accurately. But there was a page missing towards the end. On that page was the Conservative crowd pleaser of a plan to scrap stamp duty in England and Northern Ireland.

Fast forward to now and there was a familiar drill. There was plenty of chat throughout the conference and beforehand of a new policy coming on inheritance tax, and, sure enough, another page was missing towards the end of her speech with her plan on that.

The plan reopens the fascinating politics and psychology of inheritance tax – which is paid by fewer than one in 20 people, external but has been described as the country's most unpopular tax, external.

Why so? Advocates of cutting or scrapping it say it is because plenty aspire to one day being rich enough to end up having to pay it, plus it is a second tax on already taxed income.

But the Conservatives' opponents, even before this speech, were already looking forward to the argument they anticipated after it.

Reform UK, for instance, claim it is a "tax cut for multi-millionaires" and that their plan to cut income tax for millions by raising the threshold at which most people start paying it will benefit far more people.

Policy announcements aside, what stood out in this speech for me was a broader point. The veteran Conservative elections strategist Sir Lynton Crosby once suggested the party ought to "scrape the barnacles off the boat" as he put it, in reference to unpopular policies that could cause the Tories a headache during an election campaign.

This speech felt like Badenoch revelling in pointing at the clean hull of the Conservative ship, what she sees as those barnacles removed, not least the high-profile defections of Jenrick and Suella Braverman.

There was a striking glee and anger in her reflections about Reform UK. She sought to portray them as sleazy and pointedly decided to lean into an argument of recent months about Englishness.

Braverman has argued that, given her Asian heritage, "I'm not English".

"I'm proud to be British. My family and ancestors have a link to Britain which spans centuries. But in no way are we English," she wrote on social media last month, external, adding: "Englishness is an ethnicity."

Badenoch expressed her personal fury at this, saying that as the mother of mixed-race children "I don't want to explain to my son, when we're watching our brilliant England team play football, that some people don't think our black players are English".

The recurring message, today and over the last few days, is Badenoch cannot stand Reform and won't work with them before or after the next general election.

But what she said amounted to an attack on Reform's character and the judgement of their prominent figures, rather than a significant focus on the policies we hear talked about most often by Nigel Farage.

Badenoch did talk about immigration, but not at length. She largely left the issue – and the Conservative policy to withdraw from the European Convention on Human Rights, as Reform also advocates - to her shadow home secretary Chris Philp who spoke before her.

Instead, Badenoch grounded this speech in the big picture tussle to be trusted between Labour and the Conservatives – and in particular who was better placed to deliver a growing economy.

In tone, language and public enthusiasm for the argument, Badenoch and Andy Burnham are quite the contrast with their immediate predecessors Rishi Sunak and Sir Keir Starmer.

Badenoch and Burnham both look like they are enjoying themselves on the stage, and are both enthusiastic purveyors of the core of what are their very different worldviews.

Badenoch acknowledged this with what she called the "battle for the soul of this nation" in the opening minute or so of her address. It is a trailer for the debate to come this autumn and beyond.

GeneralTab.title: Boots sold in £7bn deal to Canadian billionaire family
GeneralTab.text:
Boots, the High Street pharmacy and retail chain, has been sold in an $8.9bn (£6.7bn) deal to Canada's billionaire Weston family.

Wittington Investments, the holding company, confirmed it had agreed to buy the 177-year-old retailer on Wednesday from US private equity firm Sycamore Partners and the Pessina family.

Boots started as a simple apothecary in Nottingham but has evolved to become a stalwart of the High Street, expanding its business to sell a vast range of health and beauty products, meal deals and travel accessories.

The chain has performed well in recent years despite challenges from rivals and changing shopping habits.

Its stores have seen lower footfall as people switched to working from home rather than visiting town and city centre offices every weekday.

It has closed hundreds of branches across the UK in recent years, leaving it with about 1,800 stores and 51,000 employees, but remains a familiar British brand.

In its most recent annual results, Boots generated £7.5bn in sales - a 3.2% increase on 2024.

Retail expert Catherine Shuttleworth, chief executive of savvy marketing, said shoppers were unlikely to see much change to stores in the coming months, but added what they can "expect over time is an improved shopping experience as the new owners invest in the business".

She said health and beauty was a "massive area for growth", and fresh investment from its new ownership would help.

The last two decades has seen several changes of ownership under discussion and sometimes completed.

Sycamore only owned the retailer for 18 months, and Shuttleworth said the chopping and changing of owners had been "an unhelpful distraction".

GeneralTab.title: Ex-bankers jailed for rigging rates have convictions quashed
GeneralTab.text:
Five former Barclays traders sentenced in one of the biggest scandals of the financial crisis have had their convictions overturned following a long-running legal battle.

Jay Merchant, Jonathan Mathew, Philippe Moryoussef, Alex Pabon, Colin Bermingham were convicted following trials for manipulating the interest rates used for loans between banks.

But their convictions were quashed on Wednesday by the Court of Appeal. The ruling came after two other former City traders had their convictions overturned last year, which paved the way for others to appeal.

The traders were cast by prosecutors as a symbol of banker greed amid public backlash and anger during the 2008 financial crisis.

Merchant, Mathew, Pabon and Bermingham have all served various jail terms. Moryoussef was sentenced in his absence in 2018, never returned to the UK to serve time after France refused to extradite him.

The prosecutions were over the manipulation of two key interest rate mechanisms: Libor and Euribor, which at the time were used to set borrowing costs on a range of loans such as mortgages and car finance deals.

Mathew said the "strain" of what he had gone through had been a burden on him for the last 10 years.

"Having this conviction quashed is not simply about correcting the record, it's about finally having validation that this is an injustice that never should have happened," the 45-year-old said.

"I now have two children and this means a great deal to have the record corrected for their sake as well."

Merchant, 55, added that he looked forward to moving on with his life, but said part of that would be "ensuring that those responsible for what happened are held fully accountable".

Lord Justice Edis said full reasons behind the overturned convictions would be given later on Wednesday.

The financial crisis began in 2008, sending huge economic shockwaves across the world and triggering recessions in many countries.

There was a public backlash against bankers, held by many to be responsible for the crisis, while the financial sector was protected by taxpayer-funded bailouts.

The Libor scandal erupted in 2012, when it was discovered that at the outbreak of the financial crisis, banks had been misrepresenting their positions during the process of setting the lending rate, helping to boost profits and mask difficulties.

Some 19 City traders were convicted in the US and UK between 2015 and 2019 across nine criminal trials held in London and New York.

Each of the former Barclays traders in Wednesday's successful appeal had originally been convicted of a single count of conspiracy to defraud as result of alleged attempts to influence financial benchmark rates.

Two other bankers have already had their names cleared.

Tom Hayes, a former trader at Swiss bank UBS, was the first banker jailed. He won a 10-year legal battle last year to have his conviction overturned at the Supreme Court in July 2025.

His victory alongside that of fellow trader Carlo Palombo, who was jailed in 2019, paved the way for others to challenge their convictions.

Hayes and Palombo argued they were wrongly prosecuted for what were normal commercial practices in order to appease public anger towards the banks over the financial crisis.

Pabon, 48, who had his name cleared on Wednesday, hailed Hayes for his refusal to "let it go". He had "pushed this through" for the rest of them, he said.

The Serious Fraud Office (SFO), which brought the original case against the traders, has not opposed the appeals.

Barclays bank has been contacted for comment.

The latest ruling means just two traders still have convictions over interest rate rigging - former Deutsche Bank trader Christian Bittar and former Barclays trader Peter Johnson.

Bittar was jailed in 2018 after pleading guilty and served two years in prison. He will challenge his conviction on 9 October.

Johnson was the original whistleblower calling attention to the Libor scandal but pleaded guilty on advice that he had little chance of winning at trial. He also hopes to appeal.

GeneralTab.title: Royal Mail plans to cut 2,500 head office and support function jobs
GeneralTab.text:
Royal Mail has announced plans to cut 2,500 head office and other supporting roles by the end of 2027 as it battles competition and falling demand for letter deliveries.

The cuts at the postal service will represent about 2% of the 131,000-strong workforce.

However, frontline postal workers - posties and drivers - are not part of the proposed restructuring.

Royal Mail said the workforce reduction, designed to improve efficiency, would be achieved through voluntary redundancies and people choosing to leave the company.

It said the cuts would make it more efficient.

"These proposed changes remove duplication and allow us to invest further in the service we deliver for our customers," said chief executive Alistair Cochrane.

He added that the job cuts "will not be easy, but they are an important part of building a stronger, simpler and future-ready Royal Mail for our customers and colleagues".

Royal Mail said it was in formal consultation with its unions, the Communication Workers Union (CWU) and Unite CMA, over the plans.

The CWU said despite reassurances that there would be no compulsory redundancies, the announcement was "further evidence of a company that is demoralising staff and failing to deliver for customers and the wider community".

"We urge the government to confront the reality of a collapsing Royal Mail and intervene to save this national institution," deputy general secretary Martin Walsh told the BBC.

Unite said Royal Mail, regulator Ofcom, and the government had "failed to address the serious problems facing Royal Mail, especially high competition from gig economy postal services".

The union said the cuts would not improve Royal Mail's quality of service.

Royal Mail has been struggling to meet its delivery targets for first and second class post, and has been fined by the regulator for missing targets in recent years.

Just over 75% of first class letters were delivered on time in the year to the end of March, far off its target of 93%.

Fewer people are sending letters, and the company has repeatedly said that its Universal Service Obligation (USO) – a legal requirement to deliver letters six days a week to every address in the UK – is outdated and needs reform.

Royal Mail, which is a separate from the Post Office, has faced years of criticism from politicians and the public over slow letter deliveries.

In March, postal workers across the UK told the BBC they were being asked to move or hide mail from senior bosses to make it look like delivery targets were being met.

This year, more than 100 MPs have written to regulator Ofcom and the business secretary asking for something to be done about the poor service their constituents say they are receiving.

The firm has said it is investing £500m over the next five years as part of its improvement plan.

Royal Mail is owned by Czech billionaire Daniel Kretinsky's EP Group, after his takeover was approved by shareholders at the end of April last year.

articles.title: Kemi Badenoch says Tories would scrap inheritance tax on family homes
articles.text:
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch has pledged to scrap inheritance tax (IHT) on family homes while also allowing couples to leave £1m tax-free, in her keynote speech at the party's conference in Birmingham.

Badenoch added her ambition would be for a Conservative government to abolish IHT "as soon as we can afford it", but said she could not currently propose this due to spending commitments on defence, prisons and the economy.

Badenoch also used her speech to try to make clear how the Tories differed to Labour and Reform UK.

She pitched them as the "no-nonsense party" compared to the Reform UK "circus" and accused Prime Minister Andy Burnham of wanting to "live in the past".

Rival parties hit back and said the proposals for IHT, which is levied on the value of someone's estate when they die, would prioritise support for wealthier people in the country.

Badenoch arrived in Birmingham's Symphony Hall with a message to Conservative Party members that they face a "battle for the soul of the this nation".

She argued her party is "renewed" and "coming back" as she continued efforts to convince voters that it has changed following an historic defeat at the 2024 general election.

In a nod to those who have defected to Nigel Farage's party, Badenoch said: "The Conservatives have had an export boom of drama queens going to Reform.

"This party is now the no drama party, we are the no-nonsense party."

With the party trailing Labour and Reform in the polls, Badenoch acknowledged that people are "looking through the shop window", they "like what they see" but "not enough of them are buying yet, we need to fix that".

Her inspiration for how to revive a long-standing brand was Marks and Spencer (M&S), saying they have "adapted their style for today's market and people are flooding back".

Badenoch added: "Just like M&S, we must learn from our mistakes, win back trust and make people feel good about our party again."

One of the biggest responses in the room from members came as Badenoch made clear she did not want to do an election deal with Reform.

She described many Reform voters as "our people", adding: "We let them down and we want them to come back home."

Following a section of the speech mocking some of Reform's senior figures, Badenoch said: "To those who say 'unite the right', we are not uniting with that.

"People deserve better than that and we are going to give them better than that. Character, conduct, and standards matter."

She also said she did not want to live in a country run by people who "debate whether my mixed-race children are English".

In one of many jibes aimed at Burnham, Badenoch labelled him a "Paddington Bear prime minister" who was "hoping that the problems will just go away".

In the days ahead of Wednesday's speech, there was widespread speculation that Badenoch would announce changes to IHT.

As the opposition leader neared the end of her 66-minute speech, she said IHT was "supposed to be a tax on the super wealthy" but it is "now a tax on ordinary middle-class families in every corner of our country".

She said: "The next Conservative government will legislate so nobody will ever pay inheritance tax on their family home.

"On top of that, couples would be able to leave an additional £1m tax-free and these changes mean every inheritance tax bill will be cut and the number of families paying inheritance tax will fall by more than half."

The Conservatives have estimated the policy would cost around £6bn a year and believe they have identified £71bn of savings that can be made to government spending, including welfare cuts.

Under the current rules, estates worth more than £325,000, or £500,000 if a home is left to children or grandchildren, can face a 40% tax rate on assets above the threshold.

Married or civil partners can also transfer assets between each other.

In 2023-24, 4.72% of UK deaths resulted in an IHT charge and raised around £7bn for the government.

Badenoch also said her "ambition is to abolish inheritance tax altogether, as soon as we can afford it".

Labour Party chairwoman Bridget Phillipson said: "The Tories haven't changed.

"Kemi Badenoch has shown that the Tories' choice is to do nothing to help ordinary families struggling with the cost of social care, prioritising the wealthiest instead."

Reform UK economy spokesman Robert Jenrick said Badenoch had "chickened out of doing anything big" and is "for the 2%".

The former Tory MP said: "While the Tory Party is offering handouts to multi-millionaires, Reform will give everyone a £500 tax cut by raising the tax-free personal allowance to £15,000.

"The Tory Party is looking after its own in Kensington, Reform is looking after the country."

articles.title: Conservatives united behind Kemi Badenoch - but party still needs to win over voters
articles.text:
It is Kemi Badenoch's Conservative Party now.

Implicitly and explicitly, that was the message from the Tories' annual conference, which has wrapped up in Birmingham.

It is a party very much united around her, with no murmurings of dissent about her leadership, which is quite the contrast from a year ago.

The pivot point in her time as Conservative leader so far came in her address to this same gathering 12 months back, when, amid constant chatter about the prospect of Robert Jenrick seeking to topple her, she won over the party faithful with an address that oozed confidence.

Not just that. Us reporters were given her speech script, allowing us to follow it line-by-line to help us report what she has said quickly and accurately. But there was a page missing towards the end. On that page was the Conservative crowd pleaser of a plan to scrap stamp duty in England and Northern Ireland.

Fast forward to now and there was a familiar drill. There was plenty of chat throughout the conference and beforehand of a new policy coming on inheritance tax, and, sure enough, another page was missing towards the end of her speech with her plan on that.

The plan reopens the fascinating politics and psychology of inheritance tax – which is paid by fewer than one in 20 people, external but has been described as the country's most unpopular tax, external.

Why so? Advocates of cutting or scrapping it say it is because plenty aspire to one day being rich enough to end up having to pay it, plus it is a second tax on already taxed income.

But the Conservatives' opponents, even before this speech, were already looking forward to the argument they anticipated after it.

Reform UK, for instance, claim it is a "tax cut for multi-millionaires" and that their plan to cut income tax for millions by raising the threshold at which most people start paying it will benefit far more people.

Policy announcements aside, what stood out in this speech for me was a broader point. The veteran Conservative elections strategist Sir Lynton Crosby once suggested the party ought to "scrape the barnacles off the boat" as he put it, in reference to unpopular policies that could cause the Tories a headache during an election campaign.

This speech felt like Badenoch revelling in pointing at the clean hull of the Conservative ship, what she sees as those barnacles removed, not least the high-profile defections of Jenrick and Suella Braverman.

There was a striking glee and anger in her reflections about Reform UK. She sought to portray them as sleazy and pointedly decided to lean into an argument of recent months about Englishness.

Braverman has argued that, given her Asian heritage, "I'm not English".

"I'm proud to be British. My family and ancestors have a link to Britain which spans centuries. But in no way are we English," she wrote on social media last month, external, adding: "Englishness is an ethnicity."

Badenoch expressed her personal fury at this, saying that as the mother of mixed-race children "I don't want to explain to my son, when we're watching our brilliant England team play football, that some people don't think our black players are English".

The recurring message, today and over the last few days, is Badenoch cannot stand Reform and won't work with them before or after the next general election.

But what she said amounted to an attack on Reform's character and the judgement of their prominent figures, rather than a significant focus on the policies we hear talked about most often by Nigel Farage.

Badenoch did talk about immigration, but not at length. She largely left the issue – and the Conservative policy to withdraw from the European Convention on Human Rights, as Reform also advocates - to her shadow home secretary Chris Philp who spoke before her.

Instead, Badenoch grounded this speech in the big picture tussle to be trusted between Labour and the Conservatives – and in particular who was better placed to deliver a growing economy.

In tone, language and public enthusiasm for the argument, Badenoch and Andy Burnham are quite the contrast with their immediate predecessors Rishi Sunak and Sir Keir Starmer.

Badenoch and Burnham both look like they are enjoying themselves on the stage, and are both enthusiastic purveyors of the core of what are their very different worldviews.

Badenoch acknowledged this with what she called the "battle for the soul of this nation" in the opening minute or so of her address. It is a trailer for the debate to come this autumn and beyond.

articles.title: Boots sold in £7bn deal to Canadian billionaire family
articles.text:
Boots, the High Street pharmacy and retail chain, has been sold in an $8.9bn (£6.7bn) deal to Canada's billionaire Weston family.

Wittington Investments, the holding company, confirmed it had agreed to buy the 177-year-old retailer on Wednesday from US private equity firm Sycamore Partners and the Pessina family.

Boots started as a simple apothecary in Nottingham but has evolved to become a stalwart of the High Street, expanding its business to sell a vast range of health and beauty products, meal deals and travel accessories.

The chain has performed well in recent years despite challenges from rivals and changing shopping habits.

Its stores have seen lower footfall as people switched to working from home rather than visiting town and city centre offices every weekday.

It has closed hundreds of branches across the UK in recent years, leaving it with about 1,800 stores and 51,000 employees, but remains a familiar British brand.

In its most recent annual results, Boots generated £7.5bn in sales - a 3.2% increase on 2024.

Retail expert Catherine Shuttleworth, chief executive of savvy marketing, said shoppers were unlikely to see much change to stores in the coming months, but added what they can "expect over time is an improved shopping experience as the new owners invest in the business".

She said health and beauty was a "massive area for growth", and fresh investment from its new ownership would help.

The last two decades has seen several changes of ownership under discussion and sometimes completed.

Sycamore only owned the retailer for 18 months, and Shuttleworth said the chopping and changing of owners had been "an unhelpful distraction".
